opening: In Chapter 3, we saw that replacing nonnegative probabilities with complex probability amplitudes allows distinct computational paths to interfere—reinforcing some outcomes while completely canceling others. Up to now, we have written a state as a weighted sum of configuration kets, \(\sum_i v_i\ket{i}\), and tracked each step \(S\) through its arrow weights \(\bra{j}S\ket{i}\), multiplying weights along paths and adding contributions that arrive at the same configuration.
opening_continuation: Those path-by-path calculations already have the exact algebraic structure of linear algebra. In this chapter, we organize that bookkeeping into a geometric and algebraic language: states become column vectors, transition amplitudes between states become inner products, and the arrow weights of a step assemble into a unitary matrix whose inverse is its conjugate transpose. Armed with this framework, we can state the postulates of quantum mechanics precisely—separating the mathematical consequences of our transition rules from the physical laws that govern how quantum systems are described, how they evolve, what happens when they are measured, and how multiple systems combine.
intro_continuation: Why can the very same physical preparation look completely random under one measurement and completely definite under another? In our geometric picture, a state is a unit vector in a space of amplitudes, an undisturbed step rotates that vector rigidly without changing lengths or angles, and a measurement projects the state vector onto an orthogonal set of basis directions—reporting one direction with probability equal to its squared projected length and collapsing the state onto the observed branch. Understanding how unitary evolution, projective measurement, and composite tensor-product spaces work together gives us the complete physical foundation for quantum computation.
